list.listitem: Mediastinal enlargement is defined as a total width of more than 8 cm at the level of the aortic arch or a mediastinal to chest width ratio of more than 0.25. C
The most common mediastinal mass is lymphoma. C
Rare but important causes of mediastinal enlargement include anthrax infection. C
CT of the chest is usually the recommended initial imaging study to evaluate the patient with mediastinal enlargement seen on CXR. C

background.definition: The mediastinum is the area in the chest demarcated by the pleural cavities, the thoracic inlet and the diaphragm. Mediastinal enlargement is defined as a total width of more than 8 cm at the level of the aortic arch or a mediastinal to chest width ratio of more than 0.25.

list.listitem: The incidence of thoracic aortic aneurysm is estimated at 6 cases per 100,000 patient-years.
The incidence of thymoma is 0.15% per 100,000 people.
The annual incidence of sarcoidosis is 10-12/100,000 in whites, 30/100,000 in African-American men, and 39/100,000 in African-American women.
The lifetime risk of sarcoidosis is 2.4% in blacks and 0.85% in whites.
Greater than one-half million people are affected by lymphoma (both Hodgkins and non-Hodgkins).
See Differential Diagnosis table below.

In a series of 60 patients with mediastinal masses, causes included lymphoma (35%), metastatic carcinoma (26.6%), thymoma (16.6%), germ cell tumor (5%), lymph node infection (3.3%), mesothelioma (5%), and sarcoid (1.7%).
The pathophysiology of mediastinal enlargement depends on the causative etiology.
See separate chapters on Hodgkins lymphoma, non-Hodgkins lymphoma, Sarcoidosis, thoracic aortic aneursym, and thyroid mass.

Differential.Differential_Features: May have extra-pulmonary involvement (cranial nerves, cutaneous lesions)
Presence of B symptoms, palpable lymphadenopathy
History of Marfan’s disease or blunt chest trauma
May be associated symptoms related to thyroid disease; may be palpable
Patient may have a history of tobacco use, presence of systemic symptoms
Patient may have a history of myasthenia gravis

list.listitem: Physical examination should be directed at the most common and important causes of mediastinal enlargement, such as lymphoma, sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, and aortic vessel disease or injury. Lymphoma: history may include fevers, night sweats and weight loss. Physical examination may reveal lymphadenopathy. Sarcoidosis: personal or family history of autoimmune disease may be present. Cutaneous lesions, cranial nerve palsies and other neurologic deficits may be found on physical examination. Aneurysm related to Marfan’s syndrome: this is characterized by a tall, lanky stature, long limbs and fingers, flat feet and a highly arching palate. These patients are prone to aortic aneurysms and dissection. Thyroid disease: hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism will present with changes in weight, hair texture and body temperature. Nodules or a diffusely enlarged thyroid may be present on physical examination. Lung neoplasm: may cause hemoptysis, weight loss, dyspnea, cough.

Chest CT should be performed first to determine the location of the mass in the mediastinum. Depending on the results, further testing is indicated as described below. Lymphoma suspected: A diagnosis of lymphoma is traditionally obtained by excisional biopsy, immunohistochemical staining, and genetic studies, if appropriate. Sarcoidosis suspected: order serum ACE levels, and biopsy any granulomas. Thoracic aortic disease: order is best confirmed by CT, MRI, angiography, or transesophageal echocardiogram.

Thyroid disease is confirmed by serum measurement of thyroid stimulating hormone, thyroxine and thyroid antibodies, when appropriate. Imaging with ultrasonography and biopsy or fine needle aspiration provides additional diagnostic information.

In some cases, there is a role for endoscopic ultrasound with fine needle aspiration for pathologic diagnosis of a posterior mediastinal mass. This technique can also help with preoperative staging of nonsmall cell lung cancers.
Anterior mediastinal masses can cause life-threatening collapse of the airway, making general anesthesia very risky. If possible, masses in this location should be biopsied with local anesthesia.
Beta Human Chorionic Gonadotropin and Alpha Fetoprotein serum levels can be elevated in germ cell tumors.
An enlarged mediastinum is usually an incidental finding on chest roentgenogram.
Initial imaging study for further workup is chest CT to determine whether it is anterior, middle or posterior and the likely diagnosis.

Anterior mediastinal masses include: aneurysms, goiters, thyroid tumors, lymphoma, thymomas and germ cell tumors. Middle mediastinal masses include: lymphoma, lymph node hyperplasia. Posterior mediastinal masses include: aneurysms, esophageal diverticula, bronchogenic tumors.

Solid masses generally require biopsy to confirm the diagnosis. This can be done with endoscopic fine needle aspiration, thoracotomy, mediastinoscopy or with bronchoalveolar lavage. CT-guided core needle biopsy for mediastinal mass has a 92% diagnostic yield and 94% accuracy, based on a systematic review and meta-analysis. Major complication rates are low (2%).
